introduction-the-problem-with-layers.core: Traditional architectures scale by layers: one load-balancer tier, one app tier, one database tier shared by all customers. A bad deploy, poison request or overload in any layer affects everyone. Cell-based architecture instead slices the system vertically into independent full-stack cells, each serving a subset of customers, limiting blast radius.

first_principles.problem: A single malformed request pattern from one customer crashes the shared app tier for all customers.
truths: Most requests only need one customer's data.

analogy.title: Separate kitchens per restaurant in a food hall
analogy.story: A grease fire in one kitchen doesn't close the others.
analogy.breaks: Food halls share plumbing; cells should share as little as possible.

check.q: What's the main benefit of cell-based architecture?
check.a: It limits the blast radius of failures to the customers in one cell.

defining-the-cell.core: A cell is a complete, independent instance of the service (compute, storage, queues, caches) with a fixed maximum capacity, serving the customers mapped to it. Cells share nothing except a minimal routing layer and global control functions. The partition key must let almost all requests be served within one cell.

first_principles.problem: Engineers build 'cells' that still share a global database, so one cell's overload affects all.
truths: Isolation fails if anything significant is shared.
derivation: Set a **max size** and test it.
Keep **global services** minimal and highly available.

analogy.title: Identical self-contained branch offices
analogy.story: Each has its own staff, files and phones, serving its own clients.
analogy.breaks: Branches can borrow staff; cells shouldn't borrow capacity across boundaries.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Each cell independently testable and deployable.

check.q: Why must a cell include its own database?
check.a: A shared database would couple cells and let one cell's problems affect all.

blast-radius-mathematics.core: With N equal cells, a failure confined to one cell affects about 1/N of customers. More, smaller cells shrink impact but add operational overhead and reduce pooling efficiency. Deploying cell by cell (one, then a wave, then the rest) catches bad changes while impact is small, so blast radius per change is roughly 1/N.

first_principles.problem: Leadership asks how many cells are needed to keep any single failure under 5% customer impact.
derivation: Deploy **one cell first**, bake, then waves.

analogy.title: Dividing a field into fenced paddocks
analogy.story: A sick animal affects only its paddock; more paddocks, fewer animals at risk, but more fences.
analogy.breaks: Paddocks are fixed; cells can be split or added as you grow.

check.q: With 25 equal cells, roughly what share of customers does a single-cell failure affect?

shuffle-sharding-magic-with-math.core: Shuffle sharding assigns each customer a random subset of k workers (or cells) from n, instead of one fixed group. A poison customer can only break its own k workers, and another customer shares all k of them with probability 1/C(n,k), tiny for modest n and k. With client retries across their shard, most customers are unaffected even by a poison neighbour.

first_principles.problem: In simple sharding, a noisy customer takes down every other customer in its shard.
truths: Full overlap is what causes shared outage.
Retries across a shard avoid failed members.

analogy.title: Giving each guest a random pair of keys to rooms
analogy.story: If one guest jams their rooms, almost no other guest has exactly the same pair.
analogy.breaks: Guests pick which key to try; systems need client-side retry logic.

example.title: Combinatorics
flow: Odds another customer fully shares a poison shard: 1 in 75M

check.q: How many shuffle shards are possible with 8 workers and 2 per customer?

cell-lifecycle-and-operations.core: Operating cells means automating everything: provisioning new cells from templates (IaC), placing and migrating customers between cells (with data migration and dual-write or cut-over), deploying in waves with automated rollback, monitoring per cell, and retiring or splitting cells as they reach capacity. Without automation, cells multiply toil.

first_principles.problem: A team builds 10 cells by hand, and now every change takes ten times as long.

analogy.title: Running a franchise network
analogy.story: Standard store blueprints, a system for assigning customers to stores, and the ability to open or move stores.
analogy.breaks: Franchises open stores over months; cells should be created in hours.

example.title: Adding a cell
flow: Placement sends new tenants to cell 21

check.q: Why is automation essential for cell-based architecture?
check.a: Every operation repeats across many cells, so manual work multiplies toil and inconsistency.
